cap.n0: One word: eucalyptus.|Five tokens in GPT-4's tokenizer, one in GPT-4o's.|What changed?
cap.n2: Last time, models got big and expensive.|Today, the unit they are counted in.|This is Professor Yufei Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego,|Lecture 1.
cap.c1: So first, why do we want to understand tokenization?
cap.n3: Because a model never reads letters.|It never reads words either. It reads numbers.
cap.n4: Picture a library card catalogue:|a cabinet of numbered drawers.|It is built once, and then it is fixed.
cap.n5: That is a tokenizer.|It turns text into a list of whole numbers, and back.|Each number is a token,|and points to one entry in a fixed vocabulary.
cap.n6: Her sample sentence: Hello students!|Tokenization is the foundation of LLMs.|55 characters. 13 tokens.
cap.n7: Look at the pieces. Token is one.|ization is another. Then L, then LM, then s.|Sometimes a token is a whole word, sometimes a scrap of one.
cap.n8: Why count them? Prices are per token. The context window,|how much text the model can take in at once,|is counted in tokens.|And the model does work for every token.
cap.c2b: And all these kind of model complexities are|also calculated based on the number of tokens.
cap.c3: So less is better. But is less always better? No.
cap.n10: If every sentence were one token,|the model would learn nothing.|So the real question is: which drawers does the cabinet get?
cap.n11: Her slide gives three answers.|One: a drawer for every whole word.
cap.c5b: So you may have some new words,
cap.n12: Easy to read, but the list is huge,|and a new word or a typo isn't in it.
cap.n13: Two: a drawer for every single character.|Nothing is ever missing, but the sequences get long.
cap.n14: Three: subwords, in between.|Byte-pair encoding builds them bottom-up.|That is Sennrich and colleagues, 2015.
cap.n15: Unigram goes top-down:|start with a huge list and prune what helps least.|That is Kudo, 2018.
cap.n16: And one red-pen note on the Gemini line.|SentencePiece, yes. Unigram: not stated.
cap.n17: Now, how byte-pair encoding chooses its drawers.|BPE started in 1994 as a data-compression trick.|The recipe has four steps.
cap.n18: Split into letters. Count every neighbouring pair.|Glue the most frequent pair into a new piece.|Repeat until the list is big enough.
cap.n19: Her practice word list.|Low, five times. Lower, twice.|Newest, six times. Widest, three times. The target is 13.
cap.n20: Start with letters only. That is ten drawers.
cap.n21: Round one. Count the pairs.|e-s appears 6 plus 3: 9 times.
cap.n22: So does s-t. A tie.|The slide takes e-s; a fixed tie-break rule decides.
cap.n23: Glue: that is a merge.|Every e-s, in every word, becomes one tile.|The cabinet gets a new drawer: es.
cap.n25: Round three. l-o, 5 plus 2: 7 times.|o-w ties at 7. The slide takes l-o: lo.
cap.n27: est got its own tile because it kept showing up.|That's the whole idea: what's frequent gets glued.
cap.n28: You don't do this by hand.|Her slide shows tiktoken, OpenAI's tokenizer library,|and Hugging Face's tokenizers library, written in Rust.
cap.n29: The code loads GPT-4's tokenizer, cl100k_base.|Our sentence: 13 tokens.|Now our own test sentence: Koalas eat eucalyptus.
cap.n30: In GPT-4's tokenizer, eucalyptus is 5 tokens.|All scraps, not one whole word.
cap.n31: In GPT-4o's, 1 token. Same word, a fifth of the tokens.|The whole sentence goes from 11 tokens to 5.
cap.n32: So what changed? Both are byte-pair encoding tokenizers.|The vocabulary went from about|100,000 entries to about 200,000.|The bigger vocabulary has room|for the whole word as one entry.
cap.c9: Generally speaking, if you are using multi-language|instead of just using English,|then it's better for you to use a larger vocabulary.
cap.c11: So that's why sometimes you want|to have a larger vocabulary.|And that's also the trend.
cap.n33: One honest limit.|Tokenizers do not treat every language the same.|The same text, translated,|can need up to 15 times more tokens in some languages.|That is Petrov and colleagues, NeurIPS 2023.
cap.n34: So: a model sees numbers from a fixed vocabulary.|And context, compute and price are all counted in them.
